# Racial Differences in Breast Cancer Survival Between Black and White Women According to Tumor Subtype: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

**Authors:** Juliana M. Torres; Michelle O. Sodipo; Margaret F. Hopkins; Paulette D. Chandler; Erica T. Warner

**Affiliations:** 1.Dana-Farber/Harvard Cancer Center, CURE Program, Boston, MA, USA. | 2.Department of Epidemiology, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | 3.Department of Radiation Oncology, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, NY, USA | 4.Division of Preventive Medicine, Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 5.Pfizer, Inc., Cambridge, MA, USA | 6.Clinical Translational Epidemiology Unit, Mongan Institute, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston MA

## Abstract

Despite effective early-detection approaches and innovative treatments, Black women in the US have higher breast cancer mortality rates compared to White women. The purpose of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to determine the extent of disparities in breast cancer survival between Black and White women according to tumor subtype.

A comprehensive database search was performed for full-text, English-language articles published from January 1, 2000 to December 31, 2022. Included studies compared survival between Black and White female breast cancer patients within subtypes defined by hormone receptor (HR) and HER2/neu (HER2; now known as ERBB2) status. Random-effects models were used to combine study-specific results and generate pooled hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for breast cancer specific or overall survival. A protocol for this review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42021268212).

18 studies including 228,885 (34,262 Black; 182,466 White) breast cancer cases were identified. Compared to White women, Black women had a higher risk of breast cancer death for all tumor subtypes. The summary risk of breast cancer death was 50% higher among HR positive HER2 negative [HR+/HER2-] tumors (HR:1.50; 95%CI, 1.30 to 1.72), 34% higher for HR+/HER2+ (HR: 1.34; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.64), 20% higher for HR−/HER2+ (HR: 1.29; 95% CI, 1.00 to 1.43), and 17% higher among individuals with HR−/HER2− tumors (HR: 1.17; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.25). Black women also had poorer overall survival than White women for all subtypes.

These results suggest there are both subtype-specific and subtype-independent mechanisms that contribute to disparities in breast cancer survival between Black and White women which require multilevel interventions to address and achieve health equity.

## Introduction

Breast cancer is the most diagnosed cancer among U.S. women and the second leading cause of cancer death.1 While breast cancer mortality rates have declined steadily over the last 40 years, declines started earlier and have been steeper in White women vs. Black women, leading to the current 40% mortality disparity.2 Higher mortality rates and poorer survival among Black women are attributable to multiple factors stemming from systemic racism including socioeconomic inequality, delays in diagnosis, and inadequate access to timely quality cancer treatment.3 Biological characteristics of tumors and differences in their distribution across racial/ethnic groups may also contribute to observed disparities.4

Importantly, though it is often discussed as a single disease, breast cancer has multiple subtypes that differ in risk factors, treatment, and prognosis.5,6 Clinically, subtypes are defined by the absence or presence of hormone receptors, specifically estrogen (ER) and progesterone (PR), as well as expression levels of human epidural growth receptor 2 (HER2; now known as ERBB2).7 HR+/HER2+ tumors tend to be higher grade, and are somewhat more aggressive than HR+/HER2− tumors. Data consistently demonstrate that tumors that express ER and/or PR (HR+) have a more favorable prognosis than those that express neither ER, PR, or HER2 (triple negative; HR−/HER2−).8 The prevalence of these subtypes varies by race, with a lower frequency of HR+/HER− tumors and a higher frequency of HR−/HER2− tumors among Black compared to White women.9 Yet, the higher prevalence of HR−/HER2− breast cancer among Black women contributes to, but does not explain, the racial disparity in mortality.10

There is some evidence that the magnitude of racial disparities in breast cancer survival differs by subtype. Despite the availability of effective hormonal therapies, our previous work has demonstrated that among patients treated for breast cancer at one of eight US comprehensive cancer centers, Black women were 1.76 times more likely to die from HR+/HER2− breast cancer (HR: 1.76; 95% CI 1.38–2.24) than White women, while in this same study there was no difference in survival among women with HR−/HER2− tumors (HR: 1.04; 95% CI 0.91–1.19).10,11 Similarly, a population-based study using data from the Georgia Cancer Registry found poorer survival among Black women with HR+/HER2− breast cancer (HR: 1.76; 95% CI 1.38–2.24), but not HR−/HER2− tumors (HR: 1.04; 95% CI 0.91–1.19).12 While at least one study has observed poorer survival among Black women with HR−/HER2− tumors,13 there seems to be a pervasive belief within the field that disparities are worse among the more treatable subtypes like HR+ tumors. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to identify to what extent racial disparities in breast cancer survival are subtype specific. Based on its amenability to early detection and the variety of targeted therapies available,14,15 we hypothesized that the greatest racial differences in survival would be observed among those with HR+ tumors.

## Methods

### Overview

We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies examining racial differences in breast cancer survival by subtype. This study did not require institutional review board approval because it utilizes publicly available data sources and individual-level patient data was not examined. A protocol for this review was developed using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) reporting guidelines16 and registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO)17 (CRD42021268212).

### Search Strategy

A systematic search was conducted of PubMed for articles published from January 1, 2000 until December 31, 2022. The following search terms were used: (breast cancer) AND (survival OR mortality) AND (race OR racial OR Black OR African American). The reference lists of identified articles were then manually searched to identify potentially relevant omitted citations. Literature searches were completed in August 2022 and then updated in June 2023. The full Pubmed search strategy is available in Supplementary Table 1.

### Inclusion Criteria

Retrospective and observational studies (i.e., cohort, case-control) or prospective trials were included if they reported the association of race, comparing Black vs. White female adults with stage I-IV breast cancer, with the risk of breast cancer-specific survival (BCSS) or overall survival (OS) according to subtypes defined by estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and/or HER2/neu (HER2). Tumors that expressed ER and/or PR were considered hormone receptor positive (HR+), while those that did not express ER or PR were considered HR negative (HR−). Subtypes examined included HR+/HER2+, HR+/HER2−, HR−/HER2+, HR−/HER2−. We placed no restrictions on study setting or size. As race is socially constructed and definitions and composition of groups varies by place, we included only US-based studies.18 Included studies were limited to those reporting hazard ratios (HRs) and their corresponding 95% confidence intervals. If the same database (e.g. SEER) was used in multiple publications, we included those that reported non-overlapping time periods, and if there was overlap, we selected the most recent study. Studies reporting results only among stage IV patients or published in a language other than English were excluded.

### Study Selection

Study selection was performed in several stages. First, three authors (J.M.T., M.H., and E.T.W) conducted independent searches and screened study titles and abstracts producing a list of potential articles for inclusion. Second, these independent lists were combined, and full-text articles were obtained and reviewed by all three authors. Third, a consensus conference was held in dyads (E.T.W and M.F.) and (E.T.W. and J.M.T.) to decide which publications met inclusion criteria. Lastly, a fourth reviewer (M.S.) conducted another search to determine if any articles were missed and should be included.

### Data Extraction

Data were independently collected by two authors (J.M.T. and M.F.) using a spreadsheet. Collected data items included PubMed ID, first author, publication year, journal, title, study population or database, sample size overall and by race, study endpoints (BCSS and/or OS), subtypes examined, number of events overall and by race, hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) by subtype. For one study, Warner et al. 2015, ETW generated an unpublished hazard ratio for redefined subtypes (i.e. luminal A and luminal B tumors were combined) to match HR+/HER2− category reported in other studies. The primary outcome was BCSS, with OS as a secondary analysis.

### Statistical Analysis

We transformed HRs and their corresponding standard errors (derived from CIs) to their natural logarithms to normalize the distribution and transformed results back to the original scale for presentation of results. Standard errors were calculated as S E = ln ⁡ upper C I - ln ⁡ ( lower C I ) 2 * 1.96 . We estimated pooled HRs and 95% CIs within in each breast cancer subtype using a random effects model with between study variance estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (REML). Statistical heterogeneity between studies was assessed using the I2 statistics. Cutoff values of 25%, 50%, and 75% indicated low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively.19 When I2 was larger than 50%, several additional analyses were conducted. Heterogeneity was further interrogated using meta regression to determine the contribution of study characteristics including number of Black participants, setting (registry, hospital, clinical trial, prospective or retrospective cohort), and adjustment for individual- or area-level socioeconomic status (education, income, occupation, deprivation). We ran sensitivity analyses using the leave-one-out and the trim-and-fill methods.20 These methods explore whether there are potential dominant studies that may have driven the results. Publication bias was assessed with Galbraith plots21 and Egger’s tests.22 All statistical tests were 2-sided using a significance level of P < .05 and were conducted with Stata v 18.5 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA).

## Results

### Study Characteristics

We reviewed 42 publications that were potentially eligible for inclusion in the meta-analysis (Figure 1). Eleven articles were excluded because no Black/White comparison of survival was presented by subtype,23–33 six were excluded due to duplicate datasets,34–39 two were excluded because all estimates were stratified by another factor (e.g. stage and/or age),40,41 and one article was excluded for each of the following reasons: metastatic patients only,42 subtype defined by PAM50,43 evaluated subtypes of HR+/HER2− breast cancer,44 only odds ratios,45 or HR+ tumors46 presented.

After exclusions, 18 articles were eligible for inclusion.10–13,47–60 The characteristics of included studies are summarized in Table 1. The studies were published between 2009 and 2022 and included a total of 228,885 breast cancer cases (34,262 Black and 182,466 White) with a range of 375 to 103,498 cases in individual studies. The number of breast cancer-specific and total deaths reported ranged from 30 to 5,734 and 77 to 3,052 respectively, though the number of deaths was not reported in four studies.

### Breast Cancer Specific Survival

Figure 2 displays forest plots with subtype specific estimates of breast cancer specific survival. Black women had higher risk of breast cancer death for all subtypes. We found for HR+/HER2+ (HR: 1.34; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.64) and HR+/HER2− (HR:1.50; 95%CI, 1.30 to 1.72) Black women had a 34% and 50% increased risk of breast cancer death compared to White women respectively. Black women with HR−/HER2+ tumors had a 20% higher risk of breast cancer death (HR, 1.20; 95% CI, 1.00 to 1.43) than White women. We also observed higher risk of breast cancer death among Black women with HR−/HER2− tumors (HR, 1.17; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.25).

We observed significant heterogeneity in analyses of HR+/HER2− (I2=50.2%) subtype. Heterogeneity was further examined through Galbraith plots, where in the absence of heterogeneity, we would expect 95% of the studies to lie within the 95% CI shaded region on each graph. Only one of six included studies lay outside of the shaded region for HR+/HER2− subtype (Supplementary Figure 1). In meta regression analyses our pre-specified characteristics, setting, adjustment for SES, and number of Black participants, explained much (R2=48.4%) of the between study variance, with the residual I2 after accounting for these factors attenuated to 16.1% (low) (Supplementary Table 2). Leave-one-out analyses (Supplementary Figure 2) with the summary estimate if each study were excluded demonstrated that the biggest change would occur with HR+/HER2+ tumors should Tao et al (2015) be removed, with the HR increasing from 1.34 to 1.62 (95% CI, 1.44 to 1.69). With respect to publication bias, Egger’s tests showed no evidence of bias for HR−/HER2+(p=0.24), HR+/HER2− (p=0.44), HR+/HER2+ (p=0.98), or HR−/HER2− (p=0.67) subtypes.

In supplementary analyses of ER and ER/PR subtypes (Supplementary Figure 3) we found that among women with ER+ tumors Black individuals were 55% more likely to die from breast cancer as compared to White (HR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.35 to 1.77). In three studies reporting results among ER− tumors, we observed no survival difference between White and Black (HR, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.88 to 1.23) individuals. Black women were more than two times as likely to die from ER+PR+ (HR 2.21; 95% CI, 0.68 to 7.14), though this did not reach statistical significance. ER−/PR− tumors were not analyzed as only one study was identified.

### Overall Survival

Figure 3 shows forest plots of subtype-specific estimates for overall mortality. Overall survival was worse for Black women than White women across all examined subtypes, though estimates for HR−/HER2+ tumors did not reach statistical significance. Black women were 33% [HR+/HER2+ (HR: 1.33; 95% CI, 1.09 to 1.62)], 32% [HR+/HER2− (HR: 1.32; 95% CI, 1.12 to 1.56)], 73% [HR−/HER2+ (HR 1.73; 95% CI, 0.94 to 3.19)], and 23% [HR−/HER2− (HR: 1.23; 95% CI, 1.06 to 1.42)] more likely to die within each subtype group.

We observed significant heterogeneity in analyses of HR−/HER2+ (I2=61.1%), and HR−/HER2− (I2=50.7%) subtypes. In Galbraith plots, two studies lie outside of the shaded region for HR−/HER2+, and one for HR−/HER2− analyses (Supplementary Figure 4). In meta regression analyses, setting, adjustment for SES, and number of Black participants explained 97.5% (HR−/HER2+) and 100% (HR−/HER2−), of the between-study variance (Supplementary Table 2). The residual I2 was 2.6% (HR−/HER2+) and 0.0% (HR−/HER2−) after accounting for these factors. In both studies, adjustment for SES was significantly associated with between-study heterogeneity in meta-regression, while number of Black participants also was significant for HR−/HER2− tumors. Results for HR−/HER2− tumors did not vary much when individual studies were excluded (Supplementary Figure 5). However, among HR−/HER2+ tumors removing one study led to summary HRs between 1.38 (Zhao et al., 2020 removed) and 2.34 (Warner et al., 2015 removed). With respect to publication bias, Egger’s tests showed no evidence of bias for HR+/HER2− (p=0.08), HR+/HER2+ (p=1.00), or HR−/HER2− (p=0.13) subtypes, while there was evidence of bias for HR−/HER2+(p=0.002). Trim fill analyses for HR−/HER2+ tumors further supported the finding of publication bias, with 2 studies imputed reducing the estimate from 1.73 (0.94, 3.19) to 1.22 (0.65, 2.29).

In supplementary analyses of ER and ER/PR subtypes (Supplementary Figure 6) we found no racial difference in overall survival among women with ER− (HR: 0.98; 95% CI, 0.92 to 1.06) or ER−/PR− (HR, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.80 to 1.35) breast cancer. There was also no difference among women with ER+/PR+ tumors (HR, 1.56; 95% CI, 0.81 to 2.98), while Black women with ER+ (HR: 1.27; 95% CI, 1.14 to 1.41) had a higher risk of death compared to White women.

## Discussion

In this meta-analysis, Black women had worse survival (BCSS or OS) compared to White women after a diagnosis of breast cancer for all subtypes examined. The magnitude of racial difference in BCSS was greatest among women with HR+/HER2− tumors as hypothesized, though effect sizes in other subtypes were generally comparable. This was not observed for OS. Understanding disparities in breast cancer survival within and across subtypes provides insight into the causes of observed differences and can help identify needed interventions. Our findings suggest there are both subtype-specific and subtype-independent mechanisms contributing to poorer survival among Black women with breast cancer.

Structural racism, a system which unfairly patterns opportunity, access to resources, and interactions with institutions and individuals across the cancer care continuum according to socially defined racial categories,61,62 is a key subtype-independent upstream factor that contributes to observed breast cancer survival disparities. Structural racism through the laws, policies, and practices that codify it, such as redlining,63 has led to widespread socioeconomic inequality with lower individual and area-level socioeconomic status among Black compared to White populations in the US.64 Importantly, these factors lie downstream of race and structural racism and therefore are not confounders, but they could mediate the effects of structural racism on health. In this meta-analysis, survival disparities persisted despite covariate adjustment for potential mediators such as income, education, individual or area-level SES or deprivation in multiple studies, suggesting that these measures do not fully capture socioeconomic inequality and that other unmeasured factors likely contribute to observed differences. For example, they miss the historical and intergenerational effects of structural racism on SES such as social class across the lifespan accumulated wealth.65

Most studies also accounted for receipt of treatments such as surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, as well as health insurance status, but this may not fully account for access and treatment differences between groups. Quality and timeliness of care including completion of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation may affect all subtypes. Racial residential segregation, lower SES and higher rates of uninsurance or public insurance limit access to academic medical centers and Black patients are concentrated in a relatively small number of US hospitals.66,67 Black patients are more likely to receive care in facilities with lower quality ratings,68 and hospitals that serve larger proportions of Black patients have lower revenues66 and offer a more limited array of services.69 Among Medicare beneficiaries, a relatively small percentage of physicians provide care to a large percentage of minority and low-income cancer patients, and these patients are less likely to receive guideline concordant care.70 With respect to breast cancer this results in higher likelihood of poor quality mammography,71 delays in diagnosis,72,73 and lower access to breast specialty care and clinical trials.74 Black women are less likely have timely completion of adjuvant chemotherapy and/or radiation treatment including delayed initiation and early discontinuation.75,76 Missed or delayed treatments may result from intensive care regimens that may require frequent weekday trips to a clinical site. Patients may experience a number of health-related social needs including lack of transportation, with paid time off work, childcare, and other responsibilities and culminate in greater experiences of cancer-related financial toxicity.77,78

While treatments like surgery or chemotherapy may affect survival of all subtypes, racial differences in receipt of treatments like hormonal therapy for HR+ tumors and HER2-directed therapies such as trastuzumab are subtype-specific factors that may contribute to observed disparities While most studies included in this meta-analysis control for treatment initiation, many did not capture the extent to which treatments are completed, particularly long-term therapies such as hormone therapy which may be taken for 5 to 10 years, or detection and treatment of recurrences. Black women with HR+ breast cancer are 17% less likely to initiate hormone therapy than White women, report greater burden of side effects while taking the medication, and are more likely to discontinue the medication early or take it less often than directed.79–83 Data also shows that Black women with HR+ tumors have lower ER expression levels, and that lower ER expression is associated with lower receipt of hormone therapy, and poorer survival.84 Trastuzumab and related medications are highly effective treatments for HER2+ breast cancers, but data shows that Black women are less likely to receive the full course of trastuzumab therapy than White women.85 Among Medicare beneficiaries Black women were 25% less likely to receive trastuzumab within one year of diagnosis than White women.86 The lack of available targeted therapies for HR−/HER2− breast cancer during the study period may explain why the magnitude of disparity in BCSS was somewhat lower in this group.

These observed differences between Black and White breast cancer patients in receipt and completion of treatment are likely due, at least in part, to the impact of systemic, institutional, and interpersonal racism on cancer care. Experiences of racism are associated with lower adherence to medical recommendations and delays in pursuing health care.87 Black cancer patients report experiences of overt and unintentional racism, microaggressions, insensitivity to concerns, poor communication, and unwillingness to offer all care options due to negative assumptions SES.88 Individuals that report experiences of racial discrimination also report lower trust in the healthcare systems and its workers, have less satisfaction with quality of care, communication, and relationships with healthcare providers.87,89 A national study of cancer patients, caregivers, and oncologists further demonstrates pervasiveness of racial bias in oncology care and the lack of awareness and accountability for these experiences among oncologists.90 Most (63%) Black cancer patients and caregivers reported experiencing at least one negative care experience with their oncologist or cancer care team and 31% said they received poorer quality of care due to their race. Yet, most oncologists, of whom 58% were White and 68% were male, acknowledged worse outcomes and poorer quality care among non-White patients, but most did not view themselves as a contributor.90 Only 38% believed non-White patients received worse communication from oncologists and most (56%) reported that it was not possible that they had unintentional racial or ethnic bias in the care they delivered.90

### Interventions to Reduce Breast Cancer Disparities

Many groups have mobilized to try and eliminate disparities in breast cancer survival between Black and White women through interventions consisting of multiple components including patient navigation, patient and provider education, workforce diversity, information technology solutions such as registries.91 Interventions like patient navigation are designed to help patients manage and coordinate care while connecting patients with resources to address barriers to care and social needs and have been shown to improve receipt of timely care.92,93 A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of interventions to address racial and ethnic disparities in cancer identified nine studies with positive effects on process of care outcomes and eight were navigation-based.94 ACCURE (Accountability for Cancer Care through Undoing Racism and Equity) included patient navigation in a multi-component intervention implemented in two cancer centers and focused on care for patients with early-stage lung and breast cancers.95 In addition to navigation, their intervention had five key components, care coordination through a multidisciplinary team, an EHR-based real time registry and alert system to signal missed appointments or unmet care milestones, health equity and anti-racism training for clinical and administrative staff, patient navigation, and race-specific feedback for clinical teams on care milestones. This intervention reduced disparities in treatment completion and survival.95,96

Community and healthcare system partnerships can also be effective at identifying and addressing community-level disparities with a 20% reduction in Black/White breast survival disparities after one such collaboration.97 Equal Hope (Formerly known as Metropolitan Chicago Breast Cancer Task Force) began in Chicago in 2008 to address community concern around increasing disparities in breast cancer mortality between black and white women.74 This coalition of community members, patient advocates, healthcare workers, and many others determined that Black women in Chicago received poorer quality breast imaging and radiological interpretation leading to missed diagnoses.98 Many of these differences stemmed from inequality in the geographic distribution of accredited facilities owing to structural racism, with few available in Chicago’s predominantly Black neighborhoods. To improve quality, they implemented multiple interventions from training of mammography technicians and physicians, to improving follow-up of abnormal mammograms, and navigation of Black breast cancer patients to Commission on Cancer accredited facilities.98

### Strengths and Limitations

Our ability to evaluate differences in survival by subtype across studies was limited by the varying subtype definitions used including use of ER only, ER and PR, hormone receptor, how hormone markers were combined with HER2, and use of immunohistochemistry vs gene expression. Use of a more consistent subtype definition across publications will facilitate future studies. We attempted to exclude studies with overlapping data (i.e. same dataset in same period), but some overlap may remain as for example some studies were conducted in states or using state cancer registries that are also reported to SEER. This is somewhat addressed in leave-one-out sensitivity analyses, but some duplication may remain. We were not able to assess or address potential biases in included studies such as lead time or length bias and studies may have unmeasured confounding. Covariates varied across studies, and estimates included in this analysis were often adjusted for potential causal mediators, meaning our pooled estimates may underestimate the true magnitude of disparities in survival. Lastly, we focused only on survival differences between Black and White women, but disparities are experienced by other racial or ethnic groups that warrant further study.

Despite these limitations, our study has multiple strengths including being, to our knowledge, the first meta-analysis to examine racial disparities in breast cancer survival according to subtype. Our analysis includes data derived from almost over 200,000 women with breast cancer including over 30,000 Black women. Combining these studies allowed for greater statistical power and ability to detect weaker associations than in the individual studies.

### Conclusions

Results from this meta-analysis demonstrate that Black women have a greater risk of death after breast cancer than white women across tumor subtypes. Our findings demonstrate that disparities are multifactorial and require multilevel interventions to achieve health equity.
